analysis.one_liner: Bans unconscionably excessive prices during emergencies and market shocks, enforced by the FTC.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 10 Senate Democrats in May 2022, the bill never got a committee or floor vote and died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it unlawful for a company to charge an unconscionably excessive price during an "exceptional market shock" — a natural disaster, energy shortage, war, strike, or public-health emergency. It would cover sellers at any point in the supply chain, create a presumption of gouging for companies with $1 billion or more in revenue that raise prices well above their pre-shock levels, and let the FTC and state attorneys general sue for penalties, restitution, and consumer refunds. It would also require large public companies to disclose their margins and pricing strategies in quarterly filings during a shock, and appropriate $1 billion to the FTC to do the work.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who face sudden price spikes on essentials like gas, groceries, and emergency supplies during disasters, energy shortages, wars, or health emergencies. Companies under $100 million in revenue are exempt, so the enforcement targets large corporations rather than small businesses. The FTC gains a dedicated $1 billion in funding, and state attorneys general gain a new federal cause of action they can use alongside their own state price-gouging laws.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful to sell any good or service at an unconscionably excessive price during an exceptional market shock, covering sellers anywhere in the supply chain — not just retail stores.

Creates a presumption of illegal gouging when a company with $1 billion or more in revenue (a company with 'unfair leverage') or one using the shock as a pretext sells at an excessive price versus the 120 days before the shock; the company must prove by clear and convincing evidence that the increase came from costs outside its control.

Lets the FTC sue for injunctions, civil penalties up to 5% of a company's total annual revenue, and damages or restitution for consumers — and lets state attorneys general bring the same actions for their residents, without overriding stricter state laws.

Requires large public companies to report in SEC filings, during and after a market shock, how much of their revenue increase came from higher prices versus costs, including a detailed explanation of their pricing strategy.
Appropriates $1 billion to the FTC through fiscal 2032 to investigate and enforce the new rules.

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations — companies with over $100 million in revenue that raise prices during a market shock beyond what rising costs justify — would face civil penalties, lawsuits, and restitution orders. Public companies would bear new compliance costs for quarterly margin and pricing disclosures. Ordinary taxpayers would fund the $1 billion FTC appropriation. Some economists would argue enforcement that blunts price signals during shortages can worsen supply problems, a cost that falls back on consumers.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large corporations raising prices in crises

drawbacks.text: Defining an 'unconscionably excessive' price requires the FTC to write rules on what counts as a market and an excessive price within 180 days, and businesses and some economists argue that capping prices during shortages can suppress supply and make goods harder to find when they are scarcest.

The exemption for companies under $100 million in revenue draws a bright line that could shield some firms while exposing large ones to penalties even when their price increases trace to genuine cost pressures beyond their control — mitigated, but not eliminated, by the cost-based defenses.
The bill appropriates $1 billion to the FTC and adds litigation and disclosure requirements, costs that fall on taxpayers and public companies respectively.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is real: state price-gouging laws exist in most states but are inconsistent and often don't reach upstream suppliers, and this bill would create a federal backstop that follows price spikes up the supply chain and gives the FTC and state attorneys general power to win refunds. The main honest objection is economic — that price controls during shortages can discourage supply — and the bill tries to answer it by allowing cost-based defenses, which means a seller who genuinely passed through higher input costs is not a violator. The disclosure section is low-cost transparency aimed at showing whether rising margins or rising costs drove inflation. On balance the design is targeted rather than sweeping, with the burden concentrated on billion-dollar firms during emergencies.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, no action was ever taken on it, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on May 12, 2022, joined by nine Democratic and allied colleagues — eight of 48 Senate Democrats and the chamber's one Independent, Sen. Bernie Sanders.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died with the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large retailers, energy companies, and other big sellers that raise prices during emergencies are better off: no federal price-gouging ban or new FTC enforcement authority exists, and no corporate margin-disclosure requirement was enacted. Consumers continue to rely on the patchwork of state price-gouging laws.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large companies that raise prices in crises

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban unconscionably excessive pricing during market shocks and referred it to committee.

for.name: 9 of 48 Senate Democrats and Independents
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no Republicans joined.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Retail, oil, and business trade associations
against.role: Industry groups opposing federal price-gouging legislation
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal price-gouging bans during the 2022 inflation debate, arguing price caps distort markets and punish legitimate cost pass-through.

sides.party_line_note: All ten sponsors were Democrats or allied Independents — 9 of the 50 Senate Democrats and Independents — no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced past referral to the committee.

industries.industry: Large retailers and consumer goods sellers ($100M+ revenue)
industries.note: They would face a presumption of illegal gouging if they priced above their pre-shock average during a market shock and could face penalties up to 5% of their parent company's annual revenue, plus consumer restitution. The industry's interest in higher shock-period prices is the direct cost to consumers buying essentials.

Energy price spikes were the bill's most visible target — the definitions explicitly cover power failures and energy shortages. Sellers at any point in the fuel supply chain, not just gas stations, could be sued.

New quarterly disclosure obligations during market shocks: margin breakdowns, the price-versus-cost split of revenue growth, and a narrative explanation of pricing strategy. Compliance cost, plus political exposure if filings show large margin gains during a shock.
A $1 billion appropriation through 2032 and a new enforcement statute with independent litigation authority. The agency's enforcement role runs alongside the consumer interest the bill protects.
Exempt from the ban outright, and also protected from large firms' gouging upstream in the supply chain that inflates their input costs.
